newsitem.title: UK: Major rejects opposition call for sleaze inquiry.
newsitem.headline: Major rejects opposition call for sleaze inquiry.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major on Wednesday rejected an opposition demand for a public inquiry headed by a judge to investigate allegations against a former minister of getting cash for asking parliamentary questions.

Labour Party leader Tony Blair and Paddy Ashdown, head of the Liberal Democrats, in a joint letter told Major that only such an inquiry would "attract the public confidence which the situation requires.
"We are doing so (writing to you) because of the widespread public concern at the damage being done to our democratic system," the letter said.

But Major, who has already asked Parliamentary Standards Commissioner Sir Gordon Downey to investigate the allegations against former Conservative minister Neil Hamilton, said the House of Commons was capable of dealing with its own affairs.

"The inquiry by Sir Gordon Downey is under way. If Sir Gordon requires additional manpower or other resources to carry out his investigation, I have already made clear that he should have them. I hope you would support that too."

Hamilton resigned in 1994 after he was accused of accepting money from Mohammed al-Fayed, the Egyptian-born owner of London's luxury Harrods store, in return for tabling a series of questions in parliament.
He admitted accepting payments totalling 10,000 pounds ($15,600) from parliamentary lobbyist Ian Greer, who also handed out money to around 30 other predominantly Conservative members of parliament.

Last week, just days before the ruling Conservatives began their last annual conference before an election due by next May, Hamilton dropped a libel case against the Guardian newspaper on the eve of the trial in which Major and Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine had been called as witnesses.
Blair and Ashdown said a memo reportedly written by David Willetts, a Major aide, suggests an attempt was made in 1994 to undermine investigations into the allegations against Hamilton.
Four newspaper said Willetts had sent a confidential memorandum in 1994 to senior Conservatives outlining ways in which the investigation could be halted or toned down.

"The document suggests political interference in a committee which had a quasi-judicial role. It will raise in the public mind fears that there may be attempts to bring similar pressures to bear on the Committe of Standards and Privileges," the joint letter said.
